Sceptre
sĕp´ter
n. (a royal staff, the emblem of sovereign authority; rendering Hebrew shebet, sharbit, Greek rhabdos)
From Greek skeptron, a staff to lean on, through Latin sceptrum. The Hebrew shebet means both a rod of rule and a tribe — a people gathered under one staff.

Biblical Definition

Sceptre is the emblem of the right to rule, and Scripture makes it a messianic word from Genesis onward. Jacob's blessing on Judah is the hinge of Old Testament expectation: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be” (Gen 49:10). Balaam — a hired prophet who could not curse — sees the same thing: “there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel” (Num 24:17). The Psalter then addresses the King as God and describes His rule by its quality: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre” (Psa 45:6) — a verse Hebrews applies directly to the Son. Esther supplies the human picture that makes the doctrine felt: no one may approach the king uncalled and live, “except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre” (Est 4:11). Access is a gift of the sceptre, never a right of the petitioner.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a sceptre as a staff or baton borne by kings on solemn occasions as a badge of authority, and hence as royal power or sovereignty itself.

expand to see more

SCEP´TER, n. A staff or baton borne by kings on solemn occasions, as a badge of authority.

Hence, 2. The appropriate ensign of royalty; and figuratively, royal power or authority.

The sceptre shall not depart from Judah. Gen. xlix.

SCEP´TER, v.t. To invest with royal authority, or with the ensign of authority.

Key Scripture

Gen 49:10 — "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be."

Psa 45:6 — "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre."

Num 24:17 — "I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth."

Est 4:11 — "All the king's servants, and the people of the king's provinces, do know, that whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days."

Modern Corruption

The lordship of Christ reduced to a private preference — a sceptre over the inner life only — where Scripture makes it a public rule to which the gathering of the peoples belongs.

expand to see more

The modern settlement permits Christ a sceptre over the heart and the congregation and denies Him one anywhere else. But Genesis 49:10 says the gathering of the peoples is to Him, and Psalm 45:6 calls the sceptre of His kingdom a right sceptre — a standard of rule, not a private devotion. A confession that Jesus is Lord of the believer's feelings and of nothing outside them is not a smaller version of the biblical claim; it is a different claim.

Esther 4:11 is where the doctrine turns pastoral, and it is the passage to recover. In Persia, approaching the king uncalled was death unless he extended the golden sceptre. That is the natural position of every sinner before God, and it explains why access is always spoken of as a mercy. The believer comes boldly — but boldly because the sceptre has been extended in Christ, not because the throne room was ever open by right. Esther's if I perish, I perish is what approach costs without a mediator.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shebet (H7626), a rod, staff, sceptre — and also a tribe; sharbit (H8275), the Persian golden sceptre of Esther; Greek rhabdos (G4464), a rod — the rod of iron in Revelation.

expand to see more

Hebrew shebet (H7626) — rod, staff, sceptre, and tribe; the sceptre that shall not depart from Judah (Gen 49:10).

Hebrew sharbit (H8275) — a sceptre; used only in Esther, of the golden sceptre held out to grant life (Est 4:11; Est 5:2).

Greek rhabdos (G4464) — a rod, staff, sceptre; Heb 1:8 applies Psa 45:6 to the Son, a sceptre of righteousness.

Usage

"“The sceptre shall not depart from Judah… until Shiloh come” — the hinge of Old Testament expectation."

"“The sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre” — a standard of rule, not a preference."

"“Except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre” — access is a gift."
